title: Open Source Intelligence Researcher
content:
Rappler are seeking an experienced Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) Researcher to join their digital forensics team. This role plays a critical part in executing digital forensics and investigative research to uncover disinformation trends and provide actionable intelligence. You will work closely with editorial units, revenue teams, and brand partners to gather, analyze, and visualize complex datasets that support investigative journalism and revenue-generating data consultancy services.

You are a data-driven investigator with a passion for uncovering the truth within complex information ecosystems. You have a sharp eye for digital footprints and the analytical rigor to incorporate technical and business requirements into deep-dive research.

As a methodical researcher, you know exactly when and why to use specific OSINT tools, always approaching a problem with a clear research goal as your driving factor. You are as comfortable diving into raw datasets and coordinating with institutional sources as you are translating findings for non-technical stakeholders.

title: Asia Editor
content:
Semafor is expanding across Asia to help decision-makers in the region and around the world make sense of the region’s rapidly shifting dynamics in trade, technology, finance, geopolitics and global power, in the primary theater where the new global economy is being built.

We want to connect the dots across this complex landscape, delivering rigorous, independent business journalism to the world’s most discerning readers and are looking for a talented journalist with deep knowledge of China and the Asia-Pacific region to help lead an expansion effort across digital platforms and live journalism.

A seasoned leader with a track record of managing teams, the successful candidate will bring a deep understanding of the economic and financial forces transforming Asia — with a focus on how China is reshaping the region and the world.

title: Do You Have ‘the OSINT Mindset’?: Try Our Quiz for Those Who Like ‘a Little Light Online Sleuthing’
content:
OSINT, visual investigations, digital sleuthing: however you refer to the field, it’s become a hugely significant part of investigative journalism in recent years. From finding initial leads, to building evidence relevant to an existing hypothesis, to verifying a piece of evidence found on social media – these skills can be used in many different ways for investigative reporting.

At the Centre for Investigative Journalism, we’ve been delivering training on these techniques for more than a decade to journalists and other researchers investigating in the public interest. What this experience has taught us, in turn, is that the core OSINT mindset is the most important learning goal.

While there is, of course, great value in learning tools and techniques that allow you to conduct online investigative research more effectively and efficiently right now, the field is especially dynamic. Good tools that work today may be behind financially inaccessible paywalls tomorrow, web infrastructure is subject to frequent change that means certain techniques become less reliable, new platforms spring up often with the potential to make whole sections of practice obsolete.

title: Building an Engaged Community through Collaboration and In-Depth Investigations, All While Maintaining a Sense of Humor
content:
“The thing we feared the most in the very beginning, given our relaxed vibe, was becoming too serious and turning into a bureaucratic office,” says Miglė Krancevičiūtė, co-founder of the Lithuanian investigative outlet Siena.

As we speak, she is leaning against a custom-printed pillow with a tongue-in-cheek quote — “financial cushion!” — from one of their recent investigations. Fans of their work, and follow-the-money anti-corruption investigations in general, can buy the cushion in their online shop for €25 (about $28).

Image: Screenshot from Siena’s online store

Founded in 2019, the nonprofit newsroom has taken part in hard-hitting investigations led by international networks, including projects like Dubai Unlocked, the FinCEN files, and the Pandora Papers, and in 2022, the outlet became one of GIJN’s members. But its core mission is to bring that networked journalism experience home to Lithuania.

To the west of the country, across the Baltic Sea, lies Sweden, where the team at Siena draws journalistic inspiration. On the other side of a forested border is Belarus, whose internationally sanctioned dictator is a target of numerous Siena investigations.

title: Aleph Pro Tutorial: How to Get the Most from OCCRP’s Updated Investigative Data Platform
content:
Our world is data. Vast amounts of data. And this data holds many stories, often buried behind a confusing collection of documents, spreadsheets, and databases. Finding patterns, trends, and the wider story requires massive swaths of data, the ability to process it, and, most importantly, making it accessible to journalists and investigators who aren’t necessarily data experts.

This is where Aleph Pro comes in. Launched in December 2025, it’s an update of Aleph — a huge data repository hosted by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) that includes hundreds of datasets, public records, and leaks from more than 180 countries, with a cross-referencing feature that enables users to search for names and companies of interest and uncover previously unknown connections. Aleph Pro has performance upgrades, a new interface, and new features.

This tipsheet explains how to get started with the Aleph Pro platform and how to make the most of its datasets, cross-referencing capabilities, and new features.

title: ‘I Didn’t Really Sleep’: Inside the Investigation That Helped End Viktor Orbán’s Rule
content:
On April 12, Hungary went to the polls. The result was a landslide win for Péter Magyar and the Tisza party, and the end of 16 years of rule by Viktor Orbán and his “illiberal democracy.”

Just three weeks before, Hungarian investigative newsroom and GIJN member Direkt36, in partnership with Telex, broke the story of a secret operation to bring down Tisza — and secret service efforts to sabotage the police investigation into the operation.

“Neither the article nor the interview was a routine journalistic job,” Direkt36 founder and editor András Petho shared in a LinkedIn post. “They were the results of a months-long, complex investigation that we conducted under immense pressure and at high risk.” The story, he adds, was one of the biggest scandals of the election, “if not the whole Orbàn era.”

Direkt36 obtained documents from a source and spoke with multiple whistleblowers familiar with Tisza’s internal affairs — including a former volunteer for the party, a man responsible for protecting its internal systems, and a police officer familiar with the investigation — to confirm details of a secret operation to bring down the party’s IT systems and hack into party databases.

title: Bilingual Editor
content:
The Palestine Reporting Lab is seeking an experienced bilingual (Arabic and English) editor to help shape ambitious investigative, research-based, enterprise and narrative journalism about Palestine and Palestinian communities.

The Palestine Reporting Lab supports investigative and in-depth stories that uncover hidden harm, focus on accountability, and serve communities affected by abuses of power. We provide emerging and veteran journalists with rigorous editorial guidance and mentorship, meaningful financial support, and opportunities for collaborative reporting, research, and storytelling.

The Palestine Reporting Lab is not an outlet. Instead, we are a journalism incubator. We develop reporting projects, support reporters and reporting teams to carry them out, and produce and publish our projects in partnership with leading news organizations in English and in Arabic.

The Palestine Reporting Lab is a project of Just Vision, an independent, not-for-profit media organization based in the United States, and is guided by the Society of Professional Journalists’ Code of Ethics. We are committed to editorial independence, truth, integrity, and fairness.

title: Global Data Center Energy Use, US Strike on Iran School, Russia’s Security Service Leaks, Portugal’s Ancient Trees
content:
An investigation by the Sky News data and forensics team suggests that the US likely used outdated intelligence to strike an Iranian school with Tomahawk missiles in February, killing 156 people, most of them children, despite years of internal warnings about out-of-date targeting information. Our Top 10 in Data Journalism round-up, looking at stories from July 8 to 22, also includes an IStories investigation into the surveillance priorities of a section of Russia’s “second service” police force, a cross-border investigation led by Lighthouse Reports on how big food companies used lawsuits and legal threats to block public health efforts, and the South China Morning Post’s deep dive into Hong Kong’s aging population.

title: How to Make Investigations Matter More: A Q&A with the Authors of ‘The Guide to Impact Journalism’
content:
In recent years, the term “impact” has been used a lot in journalism, the NGO sector, and beyond. In investigative journalism, many newsrooms have begun implementing an “impact strategy.” But how can they do better, what is the goal, and on what practices should they rely?

It was while seeking answers to these questions for their own needs that the investigative media outlet Disclose, a member of GIJN, and the independent media outlet Rembobine published “The Guide to Impact Journalism” last fall. Available online for free, it offers a selection of best practices in impact journalism, both in France and internationally.

While waiting for the English translation of the guide, GIJN reached out to two of the co-authors to learn more: Pierre Leibovici, deputy editor-in-chief for climate and pollution at Disclose and co-coordinator of impact strategy, and Timothée Vinchon, editor and co-founder of Rembobine.

title: The Power of ‘Positive Deviant’ Data Investigations: How Good Outliers Can Expose Systemic Misconduct or Policy Failure
content:
Investigative reporters often hear from a city or department official that “We just don’t have the budget” to solve some severe problem. Or, say, claims from a hospital administrator that their abnormally high rate of medical procedures is about clinical need or patient choice, rather than profiteering.

One effective approach for holding these actors accountable is with damning contrasts: by presenting their policies and outcomes side-by-side with comparable institutions that avoid those problems despite near-identical resources.

In Argentina, La Nación exposed the needless mass exclusion of children with disabilities from mainstream schools in most of the country by digging into the model of one province, La Pampa, where 98.5% of students with disabilities are enrolled in mainstream schools.

title: Using Archives in Investigative Reporting
content:
In this masterclass, Tristan Ahtone, editor-at-large at Grist and member of the Kiowa Tribe, shares practical techniques for using historical archives and colonial documents as accountability tools in investigative reporting.

Ahtone explains why historical context is essential when reporting on Indigenous communities, land, and institutions and how to use archival evidence to expose wealth transfer and institutional profit. He walks through key strategies: identifying relevant government records and archives, connecting historical documents with contemporary data, and building sources within institutions that interact with these systems.

title: NEW COURSE ADDED: AI Without the Guesswork: Smarter Journalism Without Prompting and Hallucinations
content:
Note: Curated courses are fee-based, allowing us to sustainably support our team and trainers while continuing to provide free, high-quality investigative journalism training opportunities worldwide. The training is live and there will be no recording.

Due to popular demand, GIJN has added a third, six-hour online masterclass for investigative journalists with Henk van Ess.

There is a built-in flaw affecting every AI conversation a journalist has and almost nobody is addressing it: writing an AI prompt does not involve asking it a neutral question. Instead, you are priming the tool to answer a certain way — through your word choice, your framing, and what you leave out. The tool takes in that request and returns it to you, tidied. You read the reply and feel informed. What actually happened is that you had a conversation with a cleaner, faster version of your own assumptions.

In this course, van Ess will explain why you should never ask a bot to “summarize this,” “give me bullet points,” or “what is the main point?”
